corrected_text: THISTLE, the order of, of St Andrew, a military order of knighthood, instituted by James V. king of Scotland, in 1540, principally related by different authors. Leslie, bishop of Ross, reports, that the night before the battle between Allan king of Northumberland, and Hungus king of the Picts, St Andrew appeared to Hungus, and promised him the victory. Hungus, having gained the victory, in gratitude to St Andrew, instituted the order of knighthood. Others say, that Achaius king of Scotland first instituted this order, after having made the famous league with Charlemagne, king of France. But though the thistle had been acknowledged as the symbol of the kingdom of Scotland from the time of Hungus, it does not appear that there was any order of knighthood of that name before the order of Charles VII. of France. Others place the foundation of it as low as the year 1687. The order consists of the sovereign and twelve knights, with a collar composed of thistles and sprigs of rue interwoven with smaller pieces of gold, having pendant thereto the image of St Andrew on his cross, and the motto, Nemo me impune lacessit. The ordinary or common collar worn by the knights, is a circle of four silver points, and over them a green circled, borders and offered through pink, containing the find motto, and in the camera is a thistle proper, all which is embroidered on their left breast, and worn with the collar, with a great method over the shoulder, and brought under the right arm i pender thereto is the iimage of St Andrew, with his crois, in a purple robe, within an oral of gold canamelled very, with the former motto - but femonettes they were, existed in the June manner, a hittle crowned.
